routes.description: Establish a defensible prior framework, support the principal historical data through reliable testimony, and show that their conjunction is more expected if Jesus rose than under the relevant competing explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical sources warrant the central burial, empty-tomb, appearance, and witness data, the resurrection hypothesis has a non-prohibitive prior, and its comparative likelihood for the combined data exceeds the alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical data and prior considerations to the conclusion that resurrection is more probable than the competing hypotheses.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the relevant texts and testimonial traditions provide sufficiently reliable access to the claimed historical events.
Establish the death and burial, empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and costly witness conduct as data requiring comparative explanation.
Show that mistake, hallucination, fabrication, continued burial, and comparable rival accounts predict the combined data less well than resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply background reasons concerning divine agency and incarnation that prevent the resurrection prior from being evidentially insurmountable.
Support the durability and sincerity of the reported experiences while distinguishing those properties from the final historical inference.

routes.description: Apply demanding but claim-sensitive historical standards, challenge the reliability and independence of the proposed data, and deny that comparative or Bayesian framing can supply warrant absent adequate support for the event itself.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the claimed death, tomb, appearances, or transmission remain insufficiently established, or if the inference from those reports to resurrection fails to exceed natural alternatives and rational uncertainty remains available.

motionBridge.description: Connect deficiencies in the data and inference to the conclusion that the historical evidence does not make resurrection more probable than competing hypotheses.

centralBridges.description: Require source proximity, independence, corroboration, confirmed witnesses, and evidence proportionate to the extraordinary character of the claim.
Challenge whether death, burial, an empty tomb, appearances, and accurate transmission are independently established historical data.
Distinguish reports, sincerity, transformation, and expected evidence under resurrection from evidence that resurrection actually occurred.
Preserve an unknown or unconvinced conclusion when exhaustive hypotheses lack sufficiently grounded probability assignments.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate whether the event occurred from claims about God, supernatural mechanisms, present miracles, or other alleged returns from death.
Test whether selective disclosure, obscure testimony, and sacrificial means fit the divine background assumptions used to support the prior.

sections.title: Probability Method, Priors, and Rational Uncertainty
sections.rationale: This issue governs how the historical material may update an initial probability, whether qualitative likelihoods are usable, and whether the largest member of an exhaustive set warrants belief or leaves uncertainty.

sections.title: Source Reliability, Independence, and Transmission
sections.rationale: The resurrection comparison depends on whether the New Testament writings and underlying testimony provide sufficiently early, independent, corroborated, and accurately transmitted access to the alleged events.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and Empty-Tomb Foundations
sections.rationale: Death, placement in a known tomb, and subsequent emptiness form a central evidential sequence, while disputes over confirmation determine whether that sequence is available for explanation at all.

sections.title: Appearances, Memory, Sincerity, and Transformation
sections.rationale: Reported encounters and witness conduct supply a principal affirmative datum, but their force depends on memory, identification, sincerity, transmission, and the distinction between committed belief and truth.

sections.title: Competing Explanations and Supernatural Context
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing resurrection with mistake, hallucination, fabrication, and other explanations while determining whether divine agency, incarnation, modern miracles, or analogous claims legitimately affect that comparison.

moves.proposition: Failure to establish a particular naturalistic alternative does not establish resurrection, especially when the biblical accounts themselves lack independently confirmed reliability.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Matt, and the response consistently states the skeptical position in the first person.

components.text: Whether failure of selected natural alternatives is enough to warrant belief in resurrection under a comparative framework.
Whether the biblical accounts possess adequate independently confirmed reliability before alternatives are compared.
Whether weaknesses in hallucination or collusion explanations independently establish resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing the demand to prove a specific natural alternative with the preserved demand that the affirmative establish resurrection and reliable data.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it preserves the legitimate comparative issue while explaining why failure of one rival does not discharge the affirmative burden.

precisionFindings.rationale: The courtroom analogy clearly separates failure to establish one alternative from affirmative establishment of another conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The preserved burden claim is warranted, and the speaker explicitly allows that the accounts may be accurate while remaining unconvinced.

charity.alternative: An exhaustive probabilistic comparison can favor resurrection without deductively proving it or disproving every alternative.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative support still requires warranted data, defensible priors, and likelihoods for relevant alternative classes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference correctly distinguishes failure of an alternative from affirmative support, with a bounded analogy-related ambiguity about proof standards.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden principle is well supported by the analogy, while the further claim of inadequate biblical reliability is asserted rather than developed here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the skeptical motion bridge by preserving the affirmative burden despite weaknesses in particular alternatives.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly resists burden shifting and preserves probabilistic comparison, though the courtroom analogy may suggest a stricter proof model.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses a courtroom analogy to place the burden on the affirmative and distinguishes failure to prove one conclusion from proof of another.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even an exhaustive set of hypotheses does not warrant believing the member assigned the largest probability when none has sufficient evidential support; the rational conclusion may remain unknown.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly rejects the proposed inference and restates Dillahunty's skeptical evidentiary position in a sustained first-person response.

components.text: Whether the highest-ranked member of an exhaustive hypothesis set must be believed despite insufficient absolute evidential support.
Whether qualitative probability assignments warrant a conclusion when the available data remain insufficient.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the inference from exhaustive ranking to warranted belief and states the defeating consequence that rational uncertainty may remain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly identifies insufficient support despite exhaustiveness and states the unknown conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between exhaustive options, comparative ranking, threshold support, and unknown conclusion is clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move cautiously preserves uncertainty when no hypothesis exceeds sufficient support and expressly conditions its conclusion on limited data.

charity.alternative: Rational choice can sometimes favor the most probable exhaustive option even if its probability is below one half.
charity.decisiveQualification: Being most probable may guide action without necessarily warranting categorical historical belief under insufficient evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move validly distinguishes completeness of the hypothesis set from sufficiency of evidence, with one bounded threshold ambiguity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The probabilistic reasoning is well explained and tied to diminishing data, though no formal account of sufficient support is provided.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes the skeptical motion bridge by connecting limited data to withholding the comparative probability conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately protects doxastic uncertainty, though its reference to one-half could overstate a universal belief threshold.
